title: Corpus Juris Civilis
description: Collection of legal works codified by Justinian I of Byzantium
wiki_lead:
The Corpus Juris (or Iuris) Civilis ("Body of Civil Law") is the modern name for a collection of fundamental works in jurisprudence, enacted from 529 to 534 by order of Roman Emperor Justinian I. It is also sometimes referred to metonymically after one of its parts, the Code of Justinian.
The work as planned had three parts: the Code (Codex) is a compilation, by selection and extraction, of imperial enactments to date; the Digest or Pandects (the Latin title contains both Digesta and Pandectae) is an encyclopedia composed of mostly brief extracts from the writings of Roman jurists; and the Institutes (Institutiones) is a student textbook, mainly introducing the Code, although it has important conceptual elements that are less developed in the Code or the Digest. All three parts, even the textbook, were given force of law. They were intended to be, together, the sole source of law; reference to any other source, including the original texts from which the Code and the Digest had been taken, was forbidden. Nonetheless, Justinian found himself having to enact further laws; today these are counted as a fourth part of the Corpus, the Novellae Constitutiones (Novels, literally New Laws).
The work was directed by Tribonian, an official in Justinian's court in Constantinople. His team was authorized to edit what they included. How far they made amendments is not recorded and, in the main, cannot be known because most of the originals have not survived. The text was composed and distributed almost entirely in Latin, which was still the official language of the government of the Eastern Roman Empire in 529–534, whereas the prevalent language of merchants, farmers, seamen, and other citizens was Greek. By the early 7th century, Greek had largely replaced Latin as the dominant language of the empire.
The Corpus Juris Civilis was revised into Greek, when that became the predominant language of the Eastern Roman Empire, and continued to form the basis of the empire's laws, the Basilika (Greek: τὰ βασιλικά, 'imperial laws'), through the 15th century. The Basilika in turn served as the basis for local legal codes in the Balkans during the following Ottoman period and later formed the basis of the legal code of Modern Greece. In Western Europe, the Corpus Juris Civilis, or its successor texts like the Basilika, did not get well established originally and was only recovered in the Middle Ages, being "received" or imitated as private law. Its public law content was quarried for arguments by both secular and ecclesiastical authorities. This recovered Roman law, in turn, became the foundation of law in all civil law jurisdictions. The provisions of the Corpus Juris Civilis also influenced the canon law of the Catholic Church: it was said that ecclesia vivit lege romana – the church lives by Roman law. Its influence on common law legal systems has been markedly less, although still significant, with Latinate legal concepts and terminology from the Corpus having survived through Norman law, canon law, and civil law influences – such as the contrast, especially in the Institutes, between "law" (statute) and custom. The Corpus continues to have a major influence on public international law. Its four parts thus constitute the foundation documents of the Western legal tradition.

Compilation process

Justinian acceded to the imperial throne in Constantinople in 527. Six months after his accession, in order to reduce the great number of imperial constitutions and thus also the number of court proceedings, Justinian arranged for the creation of a new collection of imperial constitutions (Codex Iustinianus). The commission in charge of the compilation process was explicitly authorized to leave out or change text and to delete what was obsolete or contradictory. Soon, in 529, the Codex was completed and was conferred the force of law in the whole empire, replacing all earlier constitutions and the Codex Theodosianus.

grok_lead: The Corpus Juris Civilis ("Body of Civil Law") is the modern designation for a monumental codification of Roman jurisprudence commissioned by Byzantine Emperor Justinian I (r. 527â565 CE) and enacted primarily between 529 and 534 CE. This comprehensive legal corpus aimed to consolidate centuries of Roman statutes, juristic writings, and imperial constitutions into a coherent system, eliminating contradictions and redundancies that had accumulated since the republic's founding. It comprises four main components: the Codex Justinianus, a revised collection of imperial edicts from Hadrian onward; the Digesta (or Pandectae), an encyclopedic digest of opinions from leading classical jurists; the Institutiones, a foundational textbook modeled on earlier Roman manuals for training lawyers; and the Novellae Constitutiones, a series of new laws issued after the codex's promulgation. The compilation was directed by the jurist Tribonianus, who led teams of legal scholars in sifting through vast archives, often under tight deadlines imposed by Justinian to restore imperial authority amid the empire's territorial reconquests. Originally promulgated in Latin across the Byzantine Empire, the Corpus Juris Civilis initially served to standardize administration and adjudication in Justinian's domains, reflecting a blend of classical pagan jurisprudence with emerging Christian principles that elevated protections for slaves, women, and familial relations. Its survival through the medieval period, particularly via monastic preservation and rediscovery in the 11th century at Bologna, propelled it as the bedrock of civil law traditions in continental Europe, influencing the Holy Roman Empire's legal reforms, the Napoleonic Code of 1804, and subsequent codes in Latin America and beyond. While common law systems diverged by emphasizing precedent over codified texts, the Corpus underscored rational, systematic legal reasoning that persists in modern civilian jurisdictions, underscoring its role in transmitting Roman legal science across millennia.
